# How this book is organized {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-warning .review-pending title="Under development"}
This chapter is part of a book in active development and has not yet
been through the author's review. Content may change as the review
advances.
:::

This book is built as **twelve studios**. A studio is a stretch of real
research work with a product at the end: an artifact you make, date, and
version, from your first working agreement to the release decision on a
finished project. Each studio opens with a page that names its **milestone**
and why it matters, then hands you its **lessons** — short readings that
each settle one research decision and end with an **It is your turn**
section — and closes with a **milestone chapter** where those pieces become
the studio's artifact. Read, do, conclude. The twelve milestones chain, each
handing the next its material, until the last one closes on the release
decision for your finished research artifact. By the last studio you have
not read about a research project; you have one.

The road starts with you, not with a tool. Studio 1 is your curiosity's
studio: it opens with a human-only move — one thing you genuinely want to
understand, written down before any tool is open — shows why that jump is
the one move AI cannot make for you, then stretches it, tools welcome, into
your chosen research problem. Studio 2 protects it: the operating rules (AI
is your arm and your research assistant, not your brain), your role
(research director), the protocol you run every time you delegate
(SDIIVDD), the ownership that never transfers, and, with the rules
standing, the formal declaration of your research question.

The road has a shape worth naming. Studios 2–4 set your rules, declare your
question, and turn it into a declared, diagnosable research design. Studios 5–6 develop your pathway —
observational or experimental, descriptive, causal, or predictive — and put
your data and measurement under governance. Studios 7–8 produce your first
reproducible analysis and then try to break it. Studios 9–10 write your
claims down with their boundaries and turn them into an artifact ready
for its outlet or event: a paper, a seminar, a talk, or a poster. Studios 11–12 make the work reproducible by strangers, then close on the
book's special topic: directing agentic AI through the final review and
the release decision. Six arcs, twelve studios, one project.

## Choose your path {#paths}

Every reader walks the same spine, and no two projects walk the same road.
Studios 1–4 are common ground: your curiosity, your rules, your declared
question, your verified evidence base, your contract. At Studio 5 your
declared pathway picks one of five branch lessons — work yours, read one
contrast, and take the complex-designs overlay only when your design has
stages. Everyone rejoins for Studios 6–9: governed data, a first
reproducible analysis, the stress test, and claims written at the strength
the audit licenses. At Studio 10 your venue picks the format: a paper or
research note, a seminar or talk, a poster, or another form entirely. And
everyone closes the same way, through the reproducible package and the
release decision. Five pathways in, four formats out: twenty end-to-end
roads, one spine, one artifact with your name on it.

![One spine, five pathways, four formats: every road through the book

rejoin at Studios 11 and 12 (reproduce, package; agentic review, decide),
ending in a capsule labeled your artifact: released or honestly withheld;
the next study opens."}

Two more things, so the structure never surprises you. First, not every
lesson is for every reader at every moment: pathway lessons serve the
pathway you declared, and an occasional lesson is an optional overlay —
each one says so at its **It is your turn** section, and skimming what does
not serve your project is using the book correctly. Second, every studio's
milestone artifact is a **dated, numbered version**, not a box you tick:
when later evidence changes your mind, you write the next version and say
why. That record of changes is part of the research, not an admission of
failure.
